entries.title: Judge halts South Side plant operations over city, state's foul odor lawsuit
entries.summary: <p>A judge ordered the temporary halt of operations at a South Side animal feed plant that has been the source of hundreds of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2025/07/09/pullman-innovations-odor-pollution-violations-chicago-health-epa-peter-chico" target="_blank" ><u>complaints over putrid odors</u></a> for years.</p><p>Judge Thomas Donnelly granted a temporary restraining order in favor of the Illinois Attorney General’s office and the city of Chicago, which <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/08/05/attorney-general-city-lawsuit-against-pullman-innovations-odors-kwame-raoul" target="_blank" ><u>sued </u></a>Pullman Innovations in August over the odors, alleging violations of state and city air pollution laws. </p><p>The business makes an additive in animal feed used by farmers who supply eggs to food company Dutch Farms.</p><p>In a statement Wednesday, Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul said the plant shouldn’t reopen until it “addresses the odors and air pollution and comes into compliance with Illinois’ environmental laws.”</p><p>The legal order bars the plant from operating until at least January 14, when a hearing is scheduled for Raoul and the city’s motion for a preliminary injunction. Operations would be halted until a final order is issued.</p><p>“Members of the community around the Pullman Innovations facility have carried too heavy a burden of environmental harm for too long, and I am pleased that they will finally have some relief from the foul odors that were interrupting their lives and harming their ability to enjoy their homes and neighborhood activities,” Raoul said.</p><p>A lawyer for Pullman Innovations parent company, A-F Acquisition, LLC didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>The plant has spurred complaints since before Pullman Innovations took over, including some that stretch back decades to a predecessor company, Agri-Fine, which was previously sued by former Attorney General Lisa Madigan before it went out of business.</p><p>The Chicago Department of Public Health has previously ticketed Pullman Innovations multiple times for code violations. Illinois EPA investigators have also previously confirmed the smell both inside the plant and in the surrounding neighborhoods, at times making it hard for them to breathe.</p><p>One city inspector, whose testimony was offered in support of the restraining order, said he personally had conducted 160 inspections at the site and described the smell as a “foul rotten egg, sulfur odor” that “caused my nostrils to burn and gave me an acute headache.”</p><p>Some neighbors <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/08/14/south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home-smell-pollution-pullman-innovations-odor-southeast-side-south-deering-steel-mills" target="_blank" ><u>suggested to the Chicago Sun-Times</u></a> in August that the overwhelming odor might have masked the smell of decomposing bodies at the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/grave-injustice/2026/10/14/55-decomposing-bodies-found-in-south-chicago-chapel-identified" target="_blank" ><u>South Chicago Chapel funeral home</u></a>, which is currently under investigation.</p>

entries.title: Evanston/Skokie School District 65 proposes closure of 2 elementary schools
entries.summary: <p>Evanston/Skokie School District 65 administrators revealed a plan to close Lincolnwood and Dewey Elementary Schools amid a budget-balancing proposal that would also impact attendance boundaries, shutter child care and early childhood development programs.</p><p>District officials revealed the details of the previously announced plan at a board meeting Tuesday night to suggest retaining school properties as a "long-term facility strategy and vision for the future," which could include using them as flex schools or repairing them in the future.</p><p>Evanston/Skokie School District 65 Assistant Superintendent Stacy Beardsley said Lincolnwood was chosen because Haven Middle School feeder schools require the most capital investment while seeing a 33% decline in enrollment. </p><p>Most of its students would be absorbed into Willard Elementary School while Dewey Elementary School students would largely be transferred to Lincoln Elementary School, administrators said. </p><p>The proposed closures and boundary changes would save around $2.9 million annually, but force more than 700 students to switch schools, including some who had just moved to Lincolnwood after Kingsley Elementary School closed last year.</p><p>"We have confidence that this footprint is the right size for the district for the next decade," Beardsley said. "The long-term plan for the Lincolnwood School would be to secure a referendum to build a modernized Lincolnwood School that could better meet the needs of our students today."</p><p>The proposal also seeks to end the School Age Child Care program at the end of this school year, which administrators said cost $1.95 million and would need a 35% increase in what the district charged parents to break even. It also called for phasing out the district's Head Start and Early Start programs by 2029, which officials said cost more than $2 million annually. </p><p>The closures and program reductions also mean the elimination of nearly 90 certified teachers and 129 support roles cut, along with eight administrators.</p><p>In finding additional revenue streams, District 65 Chief Financial Officer Eric Miller proposed raising the student registration fee by $100 for students who don't qualify for free or reduced lunches due to financial hardship.</p><p>A vote is scheduled for Nov. 9. Administrators also will also push for a ballot initiative added to the docket for 2028 which would allow residents to vote on the allocation of funds for the properties and renovations for existing schools.</p><p>Interim Superintendent Eric Witherspoon said if the board approved the plan, it would "be the last time that you see a proposal [to close schools] in this community."</p><p>"There have been so many discussions and proposals and efforts to try to deal with our deficit, but we haven't solved it, and we haven't solved it because we have not gone directly at the structural issues," Witherspoon said.</p><p>Last month, officials announced the plans to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/09/18/evanston-skokie-parents-fear-impact-hope-for-stability-as-district-looks-to-cut-20-million-close-2-schools" >close at least two of 16 schools</a> and shave $20 million from the budget, though they had yet to announce which schools would be targeted.</p><p>It's the latest in a series of school closures over the last several years. </p><p>Last year, <a class="Link" href="https://evanstonroundtable.com/2026/06/05/kingsley-elementary-school-closed/" target="_blank" >Kingsley Elementary School</a> was shuttered amid a prolonged debate — which, at the time, prevented Lincolnwood Elementary from closing — ultimately cutting $6 million in operational costs. In 2024, the board voted to close the Dr. Bessie Rhodes School of Global Studies, <a class="Link" href="https://evanstonroundtable.com/2026/06/05/bessie-rhodes-closed-last-day/" target="_blank" >which shut its doors last June</a>.</p><p>At the Tuesday meeting, Beardsley said the school closures of two schools last year saved the district $3 million. She also claimed the move saved the district $57 million in repairs over the next 20 years, though in its cost breakdowns, staffing remained the largest portion of savings.</p><p>When pressed by board members, Beardsley said increased transportation cost projections weren't yet available, and that she would have to come back to the board with answers on how special education would be impacted.</p><p>“The path that drove us to budget deficits and student enrollment decline was paved by us,” said board member Maria Opdycke. “This is a situation of our own making.”</p><p>Board President Nichole Pinkard also briefly addressed the recent guilty plea from former District 65 superintendent Devon Horton on federal wire fraud, embezzlement and tax charges related </p><p>Earlier in the day, two former Chicago Public Schools employees <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/10/13/former-cps-employees-plea-guilty-to-federal-fraud-charges-in-district-contract-kickback-scheme" >also plead guilty</a> to creating companies to apply as vendors for professional service contracts with Evanston/Skokie District 65 by submitting “false and fraudulent” documents to win more than $100,000. They then hid thousands of dollars in kickbacks to Horton, according to federal prosecutors.</p><p></p><p>"The convergence of this report and Dr. Horton’s guilty plea reminds the board that rebuilding trust requires more than statements," Pinkard said. "It requires accountability in how we oversee this district, make decisions, and communicate with the people we serve. And it requires vigilance in our execution of these duties."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/10/13/former-cps-employees-plea-guilty-to-federal-fraud-charges-in-district-contract-kickback-scheme" >Former Hyde Park Academy principal, AD plead guilty in contract fraud scheme</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/09/18/evanston-skokie-parents-fear-impact-hope-for-stability-as-district-looks-to-cut-20-million-close-2-schools" >Evanston-Skokie parents fear impact as district looks to cut $20 million, close 2 schools</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: 4 takeaways from CPS School Board president forum
entries.summary: <p>With just three weeks until Election Day, the three candidates vying to become the first elected Chicago School Board president sharpened the choices for voters by offering up distinct views on a range of topics, from school ratings to potential school closings to dealing with the school district’s struggling finances, at a forum sponsored by WBEZ, the Chicago Sun-Times and Chalkbeat Chicago on Wednesday.</p><p>And in a surprise show of unity, two of the candidates, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/hilario-dominguez/" target="_blank" ><u>Hilario Dominguez</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/victor-p-henderson/" target="_blank" ><u>Victor Henderson</u></a>, accused their opponent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/jessica-biggs/" target="_blank" ><u>Jessica Biggs</u></a> of resurfacing controversies to harm both their campaigns.</p><p>Here are four take-aways from the forum, which included questions from an audience of students from Gwendolyn Brooks College Prep High School, a Chicago public school in Roseland.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/MQI08GaQpmI?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Chicago School Board president candidates meet for forum ahead of 2026 election"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3>Blame game on campaign controversies</h3><p>Each candidate has baggage their opponents have called disqualifying, but on Wednesday Henderson and Dominguez blamed Biggs for controversies that have followed their campaigns.</p><p>Dominguez, former deputy political director for the Chicago Teachers Union, has been in the spotlight after the CPS Inspector General <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/10/09/reopened-probe-into-cps-board-president-candidates-alleged-inappropriate-contact-with-teen-could-end-soon" target="_blank" ><u>reopened an investigation</u></a> into whether he behaved inappropriately with a 17-year-old in 2017 while working as a community organizer before becoming a teacher. Dominguez denies the allegations and calls them politically motivated.</p><p>After the forum taping, WBEZ confirmed that CPS’ inspector general closed the investigation. In a letter to Dominguez, the IG’s office said it determined that there is <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/10/14/cps-watchdog-closes-investigation-of-school-board-candidate-with-no-actionable-finding-of-sexual-misconduct" target="_blank" ><u>“no actionable finding of sexual misconduct</u></a>.”</p><p>Meanwhile Henderson, a defense attorney, has faced questions <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/09/22/school-board-president-candidate-victor-henderson-defends-disciplining-his-children-says-school-staff-should-never-use-corporal-punishment" target="_blank" ><u>about corporal punishment</u></a> after divorce papers came to light in which his ex-wife accused him of hitting his son. Henderson denies ever abusing his children.</p><p>Henderson accused Biggs’ campaign of surfacing the controversies.</p><p>“Information has come to me that Jessica Biggs is the person who's trying to drag both me and Hilario through the mud,” Henderson said.</p><p>Biggs, a former CPS principal, denied the charge and said her opponents were trying to deflect difficult questions.</p><p>“I guess I shouldn't be surprised that men who have allegations around sexual harassment, around spousal abuse, domestic violence would choose to blame me for their infractions,” Biggs said. “It’s really disappointing that people can't just take accountability for their actions.”</p><p>Biggs, who was <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/09/23/chicago-school-board-member-jessica-biggs-faces-scrutiny-over-2018-firing-as-she-runs-for-presidents-seat" target="_blank" ><u>fired from her position as a CPS</u></a> principal, has faced her own questions about being taken off the district’s Do Not Hire list. That came after she won a school board seat two years ago.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Different approaches on school closures</h3><p>A moratorium on school closures expires at the end of this school year, and candidates <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/09/17/should-chicago-close-more-schools-candidates-for-school-board-president-diverge-on-key-issue" target="_blank" ><u>diverge on how the district should handle schools with few students</u></a>. Enrollment this year has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/09/24/chicago-public-schools-enrollment-drops-by-more-than-11-000-accelerating-long-term-downward-trend" target="_blank" ><u>dropped by 11,500 students </u></a>to its lowest number in more than two decades.</p><p>Dominguez, a former special education teacher, is the only candidate who has committed not to close any schools and wants to extend the moratorium. He contends that closures disproportionately harm Black and Brown students, and pointed to research showing that <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/06/15/shootings-increased-near-chicagos-closed-schools-that-sat-empty-study-finds" target="_blank" ><u>violence increased in areas around shuttered schools</u></a>.</p><p>He favors repurposing space in underutilized schools for mental clinics, food pantries and other services. “I understand that there may be red tape and difficulties and obstacles in figuring out how to build these partnerships,” Dominguez said. “But those are the things that we work on as a school board president.”</p><p>Henderson on our <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/victor-p-henderson/" target="_blank" ><u>candidate questionnaire</u></a> said he supports school closings as an “extraordinary last resort.” And on Wednesday, he said it doesn’t “necessarily make sense” to keep “all” the buildings open. He said the district can’t be afraid to discuss the matter when the moratorium expires. “That’s why CPS is in such dire shape, because they’ve avoided hard conversations,” he said. “You have to sit with the community, you have to figure it out.”</p><p>Biggs, who was a principal when there were mass closures in 2013 and said the impact was “exceptionally harmful” and long-lasting. She did not rule out closing schools but said the community needs to be involved in the decision-making process.</p><p>She said previous closures were made top-down and if the district considers shutting down or consolidating schools it needs to first develop a plan alongside the community on what to do with empty buildings.</p><p>“Anything that we’re building has to come from an express interest from people who are going to be using those spaces,” said Biggs, who now runs a program that brings healthcare and social services to Chicago public schools.</p><div class="Enhancement" </div><p></p><h3>What’s the plan to fill CPS’ budget gaps? </h3><p>On the campaign trail and in their platforms, Biggs and Henderson respectively stress financial stability and financial responsibility while Dominguez is tightly focused on boosting CPS’ budget by bringing home more revenue from the state.</p><p>On Wednesday, all three were asked how they handle a potentially looming budget crisis.</p><p>The current board <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/07/31/what-does-the-new-uncertain-budget-mean-for-schools/" target="_blank" ><u>approved a budget in July</u></a> that counts on hundreds of millions from the state and city that isn’t guaranteed. If it <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/08/24/cps-first-day-of-school/" target="_blank" ><u>doesn’t come through this fall</u></a>, that could mean a midyear budget freeze or potentially layoffs. That would be at the top of the new president’s agenda when they are installed in January.</p><p>Biggs <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/07/31/seeking-to-reverse-layoffs-chicago-school-board-approves-budget-assuming-more-state-money-will-come/" target="_blank" ><u>voted against the measure</u></a> that assumed CPS would get more state money, a decision she said she was “really proud of” during Wednesday’s forum. She cited her past experience as a CPS principal who faced layoffs and furloughs from the district as the reason why she wanted to take “a clear stance against assuming revenue that is not available to us.”</p><p>Henderson largely aligned with Biggs’ stance, saying CPS can’t “create a budget based on money that hasn’t arrived.” He also railed against <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/10/13/long-a-foregone-conclusion-property-tax-hikes-will-no-longer-be-a-given-under-elected-cps-board" target="_blank" ><u>raising property taxes each year</u></a> to maximum, which CPS consistently does and Biggs has approved as a current board member. Dominguez said he supports the annual increase and Biggs says she does not. Henderson says voters shouldn’t “pay another dime” without auditing CPS’ expenditures.</p><p>Dominguez differentiated himself from his opponents the most by praising the board’s choice to halt staff layoffs. He also mentioned his ongoing conversations with Springfield lawmakers to pledge additional money to CPS. He insisted that there are a variety of ways to generate more state revenue for schools, including millions from Meta’s recent multistate settlement on youth social media addiction and increasing taxes on the wealthiest Illinoisans.</p><p>Biggs and Dominguez both emphasized the need to continue fighting for more resources, with the latter referencing the city as another avenue to get extra funds. And for Dominguez, his financial backing by the Chicago Teachers Union, which is almost exclusively financing his campaign, came under fire from Henderson as a potential conflict of interest in deciding future collective bargaining contracts — another responsibility of the board.</p><p>“I don't want anybody pulling my strings like a puppet and telling me what to do,” Henderson said during the forum. “I don't want any billionaires pulling my strings. I don't want any powerful unions like the CTU or SEIU pulling my strings.”</p><p>Dominguez didn’t shy away from CTU’s support, saying “folks should be proud of having the support of those educators.” His pride in CTU’s endorsement didn’t come without a jab, alleging that Henderson had “wore that suit” when he asked for the union’s support earlier on this election cycle.</p><p>Taking a less combative approach, Biggs said the various donors to her campaign, which include SEIU, which represent CPS support staff, just prove her ability to organize a “diverse coalition.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-880000" name="module-880000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>More CPS School Board coverage</b><br><br>WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times have created resources to help voters prepare for this fall’s historic Chicago School Board election. entries.title: Bulls' Noa Essengue looking to prove he can be a physical player
entries.summary: <p>MILWAUKEE — The message couldn’t have been delivered any clearer.</p><p>There was no yelling or screaming even needed from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls</a> coach Tiago Splitter.</p><p>Just a simple announcement of the second half starting lineup in the July Summer League game. A lineup that no longer included Noa Essengue.</p><p>Splitter, who wanted to coach the first two Summer League games to set a tone, explained his decision for the benching afterward, pointing out that the second-year forward just wasn’t playing with any physicality. A no-no in his book.</p><p>Message received.</p><p>“I think it was a strong message,” Essengue said on Wednesday, looking back to the summer. “I didn’t play at all last year (because of shoulder surgery) so I was hoping I would play a lot this year. And to see my playing time cut in Summer League because they said I don’t put any force or energy on the court, it was something where it just forces you to change it, to put that force out there. Do what you need to force them to put you on the court.”</p><p>That’s what he’s been trying to focus on throughout training camp and the preseason games.</p><p>His coach has taken notice.</p><p>“Honestly, Noa, he’s playing hard. He’s trying to do everything we ask,” Splitter said. “I think there were two situations where we were kind of like, ‘Noa, we’ve got to be better here.’ Other than that, he’s trying to do the right things, crashing the offensive boards, being aggressive on defense, that’s what you ask from a young guy.”</p><p>Not an easy ask, especially if it’s not in Essengue’s nature to play a physical brand of basketball. Coming from the German League, the No. 12 overall pick from the 2025 draft was only 18 when he was selected and wasn’t exactly known for his physicality growing up in France.</p><p>While it feels like a trait of you either have it or you don’t, Essengue doesn’t see it that way.</p><p>“I think it’s something you can learn easily,” Essengue said. “When you go to a new league where most all of the players are older than you, they’re going to naturally play more physical. You have to try and adapt to that, adapt yourself so you can be ready.”</p><p>Something he is still yet to prove on a consistent basis. That’s why he’s in a competition for a rotation spot with the likes of Patrick Williams and Leonard Miller.</p><p>“I’m a competitor. I love to compete for everything, on the court, off the court, I love competing,” Essengue added. “Yeah, I was a first-round pick, PWill was No. 4 (overall in 2020), Lenny is in the last year of his contract, so we’re all playing for something.”</p><p></p><h3><b>Nic of time</b></h3><p></p><p>Splitter was still holding out hope that Zach Collins (quad) and Tobe Awaka (knee) would both be ready for the start of the regular season next week, but time is running out on Nic Claxton and his injured hamstring, especially since he’s missed most of camp.</p><p>“You just got to be careful with those hamstrings,” Splitter said. “We know that there is a high chance of doing it again, so we’ve got to be real careful in bringing him back.</p><p>“What I know is right before the season we’re going to evaluate him again, see where he’s at, and then give you guys a timeline.”</p><p></p><h3><b>Final dress rehearsal</b></h3><h3></h3><p></p><p>The Bulls will close out the preseason on Friday when they host Minnesota, and Splitter planned to continue playing most of the starters — if healthy — to continue getting the roster up to speed with the high tempo style he wants to play.</p><p>“We need to get some guys to go up and down, get some game rhythm,” he said.</p>

entries.title: 18-year-old woman dies after being shot in head in Belmont Cragin
entries.summary: <p>An 18-year-old woman died after being shot in the head Wednesday night in the Belmont Cragin neighborhood, Chicago police said. </p><p>Police at about 8:53 p.m. responded to a residence in the 2700 block of South Monitor Avenue and found the woman with a gunshot wound to the head. </p><p>She was taken by ambulance to Loyola University Medical Center, where she later died, police said. </p><p>Area 5 detectives are investigating. </p>

entries.title: Fire can't slow down streaking Union
entries.summary: <p>Bruno Damiani netted two goals after Milan Iloski scored — all with a man advantage — and Cavan Sullivan set a record for teenagers as the Philadelphia Union beat the Chicago Fire 3-1 on Wednesday night at Soldier Field for their eighth straight victory in a club-record 14-match unbeaten streak.</p><p>Sullivan, who turned 17 this season, picked up his 14th assist on Damiani's first goal to set a league record for teens with 21 goal contributions this season.</p><p>Philadelphia (13-10-6) has gone 12-0-2 under interim coach Ryan Richter after he replaced Bradley Carnell at the end of May during the World Cup break. The Union started the day in sixth place after sitting last in the Eastern Conference before the coaching change.</p><p>Maren Haile-Selassie staked Chicago (14-9-6) to a 1-0 halftime lead with a goal in the 44th minute, but defender Jack Elliott was tagged with a yellow card in the 41st minute and again in the first minute of stoppage time, leaving the Fire a man down from there with his red-card exit.</p><p>Noah Allen and Jonathan Bamba had assists on Haile-Selassie's 11th goal of the campaign.</p><p>Iloski found the net four minutes into the second half to tie it 1-1. It was his sixth goal in the last four matches and his 18th of the season.</p><p>Damiani added the go-ahead score in the 55th minute and an insurance goal in the 67th, giving the striker 11 netters this season.</p><p>Damiani and defender Frankie Westfield had assists on Iloski's equalizer. Iloski joined Sullivan with an assist on Damiani's first netter and Jovan Lukic snagged one on his second goal.</p><p>Andre Blake stopped three shots on goal for Philadelphia.</p><p>Chris Brady finished with four saves for Chicago, which saw a three-match win streak end.</p><p>The Fire beat the Union 2-1 on the road to close out March.</p><p>Chicago falls to 9-5-1 at home, while Philadelphia improves to 5-7-2 on the road.</p><p>The Union haven't lost since a 6-4 setback on the road at Inter Miami on May 24.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>Philadelphia: Hosts Charlotte FC on Saturday.</p><p>Chicago: At New England Revolution on Saturday.</p>

entries.title: Bulls would love to see versatile big Jalen Smith continue spacing out
entries.summary: <p>MILWAUKEE — Jalen Smith is headed for a nice payday.</p><p>Whether it’s with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" target="_blank" >Bulls</a> or another team this upcoming offseason is yet to be determined, but the seven-year veteran is being set up to grab a bag next summer.</p><p>At least Bulls coach Tiago Splitter hopes that’s the case because that would mean his plan for how to use Smith during the 2026-27 season was executed to perfection.</p><p>Splitter detailed the Smith factor in the Bulls’ 125-104 victory Wednesday against the Bucks, discussing the shortage of centers the team has been dealing with this preseason and how Smith could be the answer to address that deficiency even when Nic Claxton (hamstring) and Zach Collins (quad) return.</p><p>“What I see from [Smith] is he’s a guy that can stretch the floor,” Splitter said. “Having a five that can stretch the floor and create space is tremendous, so you’ve got to try to use that as an advantage, and we go from there.”</p><p>Case in point: The first half against the Bucks. The Bulls outscored Milwaukee 62-39, and Smith was a big reason why. Playing center — despite being built like a stretch four — Smith led the Bulls with 11 points on 3-for-3 shooting from three-point range, grabbed five rebounds and blocked a shot. He finished with 15 points in just over 20 minutes.</p><p>But the numbers aren’t even the biggest benefit Smith provides.</p><p>Because he shot 37.3% from three-point range last season and 42.4% from long range in 2023-24, the scouting report says he’s a deep threat. That’s what Splitter wants. With athletic forwards Matas Buzelis, Caleb Wilson and Lenny Miller, Splitter wants opposing centers pulled out to challenge Smith. That’s just clearing the runway for the air show.</p><p>There aren’t many opposing teams with forwards as springy as the Bulls have, so Buzelis and Wilson have a chance to play downhill and attack the rim.</p><p>“They look at me as a spacer,” Smith said after the game. “So being able to hit open shots, create more space, create more lobs for Josh [Giddey], Norm [Powell], Matas, Caleb, they like getting downhill. And, obviously, being an offensive-rebound threat, that creates more kick-outs for them. Teams are so spaced out for me with their fives, no one is protecting the paint. It’s the best of both worlds for me here.”</p><p>Against Milwaukee, Smith also was involved in a lot of high pick-and-roll/pick-and-pop plays with Giddey, especially to start the second half.</p><p>Even with a healthy Claxton and Collins, three centers are almost a must because of how much Splitter wants to run.</p><p>Continuing to push Wilson’s development is also a must, but one that Splitter admitted doesn’t need much pushing. Wilson had 10 points after a slow start.</p><p>The prized rookie continues to be one of the hardest workers on the roster, often the first one in the facility in the morning and the last one out at night.</p><p>And while he has been playing with more consistency since the preseason opener, the scary news for the opposition is the NBA game already is slowing down for him.</p><p>For a rookie to be talking like that after less than a handful of preseason games says a lot. Splitter believes his work ethic and film study also speak volumes.</p><p>“There’s a lot of teaching, especially with young guys,” Splitter said. “Caleb is a smart kid; he’s picking it up quick. Yeah, he’s learning, and he’s eager to understand what we’re doing and to learn.”</p>
